# Software environments and reproducibility

## Learning goals

Find available software, load an environment module, and identify the commands and versions used in an analysis.

## Environment modules

Clusters provide software through **environment modules**. Available applications and versions depend on the training system.

```bash
module avail
module list
module spider python       # Available on systems using Lmod
module load python         # If an appropriate Python module is available
python --version
module list
```

`module load` modifies your environment (for example `PATH`) for the current shell. When finished, you can use `module unload <module-name>` or `module purge`; `module purge` may also remove modules needed by other tools, so use it with care.

If a command is unavailable, ask the instructors which software stack is installed rather than installing system-wide software.

## Python virtual environments

If Python and the `venv` module are available:

```bash
python -m venv ~/cbw-primer/venv
source ~/cbw-primer/venv/bin/activate
python --version
which python
python -m pip list
 deactivate
```

For workshop exercises, use instructor-supplied package versions. Heavy installs or builds should follow cluster policy and generally run off the login node.

## Inspect versions and paths

```bash
command -v python
python --version
module list 2>&1
```

Record versions, parameters, input filenames, and job scripts so the work can be reproduced. Different modules or virtual environments may produce different results.

## Containers and workflows

Tools such as Apptainer and workflow managers such as Nextflow or Snakemake can help package complex analyses, but only use them if supported by the workshop environment. Do not assume Docker can run on shared HPC nodes.

## Exercise

1. Display available modules and the currently loaded set.
2. Load an instructor-approved software module and check its version.
3. Identify the executable used by `command -v`.
4. Explain why recording versions matters when reproducing an analysis.
